chunks: Flex PCBs: construction, trade-offs, uses. The question: What is a flex PCB? What are its tradeoffs and applications?
A flex PCB is a circuit board built on a thin, bendable plastic film instead of stiff fiberglass.
It does the job of a cable and its connectors, but as one thin part that folds into tight spaces.
The price is that it costs more and must be designed so the copper tracks do not crack when bent.
Think of a paper clip. Bend it once and it is fine. Bend it back and forth and it snaps, because the metal wears out a little each time. Flex copper tracks behave the same way.
A gentle, wide curve stresses the metal far less than a sharp crease, so flex design is mostly about keeping bends gentle.
The analogy is loose on one point: flex copper is a special soft kind made to last much longer than a paper clip.
A double-sided flex cross-section (thicknesses exaggerated).
The two copper layers sit close to the neutral axis in the centre of the stack, so they see small strain when the board bends.
Coverlay replaces soldermask, with an opening at the left end exposing pads or fingers. A stiffener under the right-hand region supports a connector or part.
The curve at the bottom shows the flexible region.
Polyimide: the heat-resistant plastic film that forms the flexible base ("PCB insulation materials and trade-offs").
Rolled-annealed (RA) copper: copper foil made to survive repeated bending better than normal copper.
Coverlay: a polyimide film with adhesive that covers the tracks and replaces soldermask ("What soldermask is and does").
Stiffener: a rigid piece glued under parts or a connector so that area does not flex. Bend radius: the radius of the curve. A bigger radius means a gentler bend.
Strain: how much the copper stretches, as a fraction of its length.
When a board bends, copper far from the middle of its thickness stretches more, and a tighter bend stretches it more.
The strain is about d over R , where d is the copper's distance from the middle and R is the bend radius. Say the copper sits 0. 025 mm from the middle.
At a 1 mm radius the strain is 0. 025/1 = 2. 5%, acceptable only for a single bend. At a 10 mm radius it is 0. 25%, a level the page treats as workable for repeated bending.
That is the whole idea.
"A flex PCB is a circuit on a polyimide film instead of rigid fibreglass, with rolled-annealed copper traces, a coverlay instead of soldermask, and stiffeners where parts go.
It's thin, light and bendable, so it fits tight 3D spaces, handles dynamic flexing like hinges, and replaces cables and connectors, which improves reliability under vibration.
The trade-offs are higher cost, delicate handling, special design rules like a large bend radius, and less density than rigid boards.
It's used in phones, cameras, medical devices and aerospace."
